title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Scooters From 2028. The EV Mandate That Takes Effect Tomorrow Will Reshape India's Biggest Auto Market.
excerpt: Starting July 1, electric cars under ₹30 lakh get full tax exemptions in Delhi. By 2028, new petrol two-wheelers won't be registered at all. ₹15,000 crore in investment is expected to follow.
body:
Delhi has approved the most aggressive electric vehicle policy of any Indian state, and it takes effect on July 1.

The Delhi Electric Vehicle Policy 2.0, cleared by the Delhi Cabinet on June 29, introduces a phased roadmap that will fundamentally change how vehicles are bought and sold in the national capital. The most dramatic provision: from April 1, 2028, Delhi will stop registering new petrol-powered two-wheelers entirely. If you want a new scooter or motorcycle in Delhi after that date, it will have to be electric.

That is not a subsidy. It is a registration ban — and it applies to the vehicle segment that dominates Indian roads. Two-wheelers account for roughly 75 per cent of all vehicles sold in India, and Delhi is one of the country's largest automotive markets.

## What Changes on July 1

The policy, which runs through March 2030, introduces three layers of incentives and mandates:

**Immediate tax exemptions.** All electric cars priced at or below ₹30 lakh (ex-showroom) will be fully exempt from road tax and registration fees in Delhi, effectively cutting their on-road price by 4 to 10 per cent.

**Graduated purchase subsidies.** Buyers of electric two-wheelers will receive a ₹30,000 subsidy in the first year, tapering to ₹20,000 in year two and ₹10,000 in year three. Electric three-wheelers qualify for up to ₹50,000, and small electric goods carriers (N1 category) for up to ₹1 lakh.

**Scrappage bonus.** Owners who trade in a car bought before April 1, 2020, for an EV will receive a ₹1 lakh cash incentive on top of the purchase subsidies — a direct financial reward for pulling an old polluter off Delhi's roads.

## The Phase-Out Calendar

The subsidies are the carrot. The mandates are the stick:

- **January 1, 2027**: Only electric auto-rickshaws and N1 goods carriers will be eligible for new registration in Delhi.
- **April 1, 2028**: Only electric two-wheelers will be eligible for new registration. Petrol, diesel, and CNG scooters and motorcycles will no longer be registered.

Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said at the announcement that no Indian state has provided this level of support for EV adoption. The government estimates the policy will attract ₹15,000 crore in investment across the electric mobility ecosystem and drive the installation of 32,000 public EV charging points by 2030.

## Market Impact

Stocks responded immediately. Ather Energy surged over 8 per cent to hit a new all-time high of ₹1,147. Ola Electric climbed more than 5 per cent. TVS Motor, Bajaj Auto, Tata Motors, and Mahindra — all of which have significant EV portfolios or are building them — traded higher.

SBI Securities identified Ather Energy, TVS Motor, Atul Auto, Bajaj Auto, Sona BLW, Minda Corp, and Uno Minda as the companies most likely to benefit. The policy effectively guarantees a captive EV market in one of India's largest cities within two years.

The exclusion of hybrid vehicles is notable. Unlike some global markets that have treated hybrids as a bridge technology, Delhi's policy draws a hard line: battery electric only.

## The Pollution Context

Delhi is one of the world's most polluted cities. Every winter, a toxic cocktail of crop burning, vehicle emissions, construction dust, and stagnant air pushes air quality to hazardous levels. Vehicular emissions are a major contributor, and two-wheelers — with their less stringent emission norms — are a disproportionate part of the problem.

The policy is explicitly framed as a public health intervention. Gupta described it as "a major step towards making Delhi a pollution-free city" and emphasised the link between vehicle electrification and breathable air.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

If you visit Delhi, your next rental scooter might be electric. If you have family there, they will navigate these mandates when buying their next vehicle. If you invest in Indian auto stocks, Delhi just guaranteed a demand floor for EV manufacturers.

But the bigger signal is structural. Delhi is India's laboratory for urban policy — what works here gets watched, debated, and often replicated. If the petrol two-wheeler ban holds through 2028 without political backlash, other pollution-choked metros like Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Kolkata will face pressure to follow. The ₹15,000 crore investment pipeline the policy is designed to attract won't stay within Delhi's borders.

For NRIs with exposure to Indian auto and EV stocks — Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ather, Ola Electric, TVS Motor — the Delhi mandate adds regulatory certainty to what was previously a demand-driven bet. That distinction matters when pricing long-term growth.
